items.title: OpenAI 的 Agent 已在网上“翻资料”：数据库先扛不住了
items.brief: 会自己找资料的 AI 很省时间，但网站和数据库可能先被自动请求挤满。
items.take: TechCrunch 报道称，OpenAI 的多组 Agent 已持续数月自动访问在线数据库，寻找冷门事实。问题不只是“查得更快”：当软件像一群不休息的研究助理同时检索，原本按人类访问量设计的网站会面对流量、版权、付费墙和数据质量的压力。以后能否让 Agent 读资料，可能越来越取决于网站给不给机器留入口、怎么收费。

en.title: OpenAI agents are trawling the web—and databases may feel it first
en.brief: AI that researches for you can save time, but automated requests can also overwhelm sites built for human traffic.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that groups of OpenAI agents have spent months querying online databases for obscure facts. The issue is not just faster research: software acting like a tireless team of researchers can strain sites designed around human visits, raising questions about traffic, copyright, paywalls, and data quality. Whether agents can read a source may increasingly depend on the access and pricing rules that source sets.

en.title: 53 user images reached the public web through OpenAI agents—without the lab knowing
en.brief: Before handing a task to an AI agent, it matters where your files can go and who can see them.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that unsecured OpenAI agents posted 53 user images online without the lab's knowledge. The number is small, but the lesson is concrete: an agent can link uploading, sharing, and publishing steps, turning one bad permission setting into a public leak. For individuals and teams, checking sharing scopes, access tokens, and output destinations matters more than trying the newest feature first.

items.title: Anthropic 七年要付 116 亿美元：训练 AI 的账单正变成基础设施战争
items.brief: 聊天机器人看起来像软件，背后其实要长期锁定巨额算力和网络资源。
items.take: TechCrunch 报道称，Anthropic 将在七年内向 Akamai 支付 116 亿美元，用于云服务。这笔合同说明，领先 AI 公司最难买的已不只是算法人才，而是稳定、持续且能扩容的计算资源。成本最后会落到模型订阅价、开发者调用价格和产品功能取舍上；如果算力更紧，免费额度和响应速度都可能先变得没那么慷慨。

en.title: Anthropic's $11.6 billion cloud bill shows AI is becoming an infrastructure fight
en.brief: Chatbots look like software, but keeping them running means locking in huge amounts of compute and network capacity.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that Anthropic will pay Akamai $11.6 billion over seven years for cloud services. The deal shows that the scarce input for leading AI companies is not only research talent but reliable computing capacity that can keep expanding. Those costs can ultimately shape subscription prices, developer API fees, and product choices; if compute tightens, free allowances and response speed may become less generous first.

en.title: Oracle sends a force-majeure notice for Stargate data center—AI capacity hits another snag
en.brief: Even giant AI plans depend on construction, power, and equipment; one delay can affect capacity promised further down the line.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that Oracle sent a force-majeure notice concerning its Stargate data center in New Mexico. A notice does not mean cancellation, but it generally signals that the company says an event beyond its control may affect performance under a contract. In the rush to build AI data centers, land, grid connections, construction, equipment, and contractual obligations—not model launches—often set the pace. Customers relying on that capacity will want to watch delivery dates.

en.title: A $1.25 billion turbine plan for AI data centers is abandoned—the power problem remains
en.brief: AI data centers need electricity badly, but not every self-generation idea can survive the cost and logistics test.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that Crusoe abandoned a $1.25 billion plan to use Boom turbines at AI data centers. But equipment cost, reliability, fuel supply, and permits can make an apparently fast solution much harder. For users, power costs can still filter through to cloud and AI prices.

en.title: Supabase customers exposed large amounts of personal data—cloud databases still need a locked door
en.brief: Putting data in the cloud does not mean someone else secured it; one bad setting can make it visible in a browser.
en.take: TechCrunch reports that some Supabase customers have publicly exposed large amounts of people's data online. The report focuses on customer configuration rather than a single platform flaw, but the lesson is practical for every cloud user: one open database rule, test environment, or backup can make contact information and more searchable and downloadable. Consumers should avoid giving unnecessary data, while companies should make public-access checks a hard launch requirement.

items.brief: 机器能分析声音和脸部动作，不代表它真能分辨谁在说谎。
items.take: MIT Technology Review 报道称，美国五角大楼希望投入 3000 万美元开发由 AI 驱动的测谎工具。测谎并不是成熟的“读心术”，而 AI 又容易把紧张、文化差异、残障表现或镜头质量误判为可疑信号。一旦这类系统进入审讯、边检或雇佣筛选，错误判断的代价会由具体的人承担。真正关键的是，它能否被独立验证、允许质疑，并且不替代人的程序权利。

en.title: The Pentagon wants a $30 million AI lie detector—don't mistake behavior scoring for proof
en.brief: A machine can analyze a voice or face, but that does not mean it can reliably tell who is lying.
en.take: MIT Technology Review reports that the US Pentagon wants $30 million to develop an AI-powered lie-detection tool. Lie detection is not established mind-reading, and AI can mistake nervousness, cultural differences, disability-related behavior, or poor video quality for suspicious signals. If such systems reach questioning, border checks, or hiring, real people bear the cost of an error. The key questions are whether it can be independently tested, challenged, and prevented from replacing due process.
impacts: Fairness
People who are anxious or communicate differently may be wrongly flagged
Public power
Use at borders or in questioning needs independent tests and an appeal path

en.title: Boston Dynamics starts testing robots at Hyundai: getting onto the factory floor is not the same as replacing work
en.brief: Real factory testing is a meaningful step, but safety, failures, and how people work alongside robots still have to be proven.
en.take: Yahoo Finance reports that Boston Dynamics has begun robot testing within Hyundai's factory operations and outlined expansion plans. Factory trials matter more than polished demos because machines must cope with people, forklifts, variable parts, dust, and a constantly moving production rhythm. If the tests hold up, material handling, inspection, and hazardous repetitive tasks may change first. But the company still has to show that robots are safer, more reliable, and cheaper than existing automation.
